title: Cap. VII: "Sinned in Adam before existing" — three denials and contradiction
pass_a_gloss: Placeus goes back to the syllogism printed earlier at page 70. The printer had duplicated three lines; the corrector, busy and rushing, left the duplicates undeleted. The argument claims: if people not yet existing are said to have sinned in someone else, then while that someone sins they themselves are counted as sinning too — and that clearly means imputation; but everyone is said to have sinned in Adam before existing; so while Adam sinned they too are counted as sinning — which clearly means imputation of Adam's sin. Placeus's first denial: that link does not clearly mean antecedent or immediate imputation; it fits better the spread of inherent sin, after which guilt and imputation come. Second denial — the major: being-said-to-have-been or died in another does not mean you yourself existed or died while he did. We die in Adam each by our own death, and rise in Christ each by our own rising; likewise we sin in Adam each by our own sin. Adam is marked only as first author and spring of sin and death flowing to us. Third denial — the minor: Paul never said all people sinned in Adam while they did not yet exist. ἐφ᾽ ᾧ here is not 'in whom.' Paul said sin entered through one man so that all sinned, not that they sinned inside that one man, and still less that they sinned then before they existed. That would put accident before subject: sinners before they were men, dead before alive, sinning before being.
pass_b_english: I return to the argument set out above at page 70 — so proposed that three of its lines were repeated by the typographer and not deleted by the corrector, so hurried was he then, distracted by other business. It runs thus: "Those who, when they were not yet in the nature of things, are said to have sinned in another are doubtless counted, while he was committing the sin, to have committed it themselves also, which plainly pertains to imputation. But all men, when they were not yet, are said to have sinned in Adam. Therefore they are counted, while he was committing the sin, to have committed it themselves, which plainly pertains to the imputation of Adam's sin." First I deny that this plainly pertains to the imputation which I call antecedent or immediate. For why should it not rather pertain to the propagation of inherent sin, which guilt and imputation follow? Next I deny the major. For are those who are said to have been in another, or to have died, counted, while he existed or died, to have existed themselves and to have died? We certainly die in Adam, but each by his own death; just as we rise in Christ, each by his own resurrection. So we sin in Adam, but each by his own sin. Only the first author and fountain of sin and death is marked, from which they flowed out to us all. Finally I deny the minor. For the Apostle did not say that all men, when they were not yet, sinned in Adam. I have already shown that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ does not mean "in whom" in this place. He did say that through one man sin so entered into the world that all men sinned, but he did not say that they sinned in that one man: and much less did he say that they then sinned when they were not yet in the nature of things. For this seems to me to imply a plain contradiction. For who would not see a contradiction implied if someone should say that the accident was before the subject, that men were sinners before they were men, dead before living — indeed, that they sinned before they existed?
source_text: Redeo ad argumentum supra pag. 70. ita propositum, ut ejus tres lineae a Typographo repetitae fuerint, nec a Correctore, adeo aliis distractus negotiis tunc festinabat, deletae. Id sic habet. Qui, cum nondum essent in rerum natura, dicuntur in alio peccasse, censentur proculdubio eo commitente peccatum, & ipsi etiam commisisse, quod evidenter ad imputationem pertinet. Atqui homines omnes cum nondum essent, dicuntur in Adamo peccasse. Ergo censentur eo commitente peccatum, & ipsi commisisse, quod ad imputationem peccati Adae manifeste pertinet. Primo nego id evidenter ad imputationem pertinere quam antecedentem seu immediatam voco. Cur enim non pertineat potius ad propagationem peccati inhaerentis, quod reatus & imputatio sequitur? Deinde nego majorem. An enim qui dicuntur in alio fuisse, vel mortui fuisse, censentur eo existente vel moriente & ipsi extitisse, & mortui fuisse? Morimur certe in Adamo, sed sua quisque morte; sicut resurgimus in Christo sua quisque resurrectione. Sic peccamus in Adamo, sed suo quisque peccato. Notatur tantum peccati & mortis primus autor & fons, unde ad nos omnes dimanarunt. Denique nego minorem. Non enim dixit Apostolus, omnes homines, cum nondum essent, in Adamo peccasse. Jam ostendi, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ non significare hoc loco in quo. Dixit quidem per unum hominem peccatum ita in mundum intrasse, ut omnes homines peccaverint, sed non dixit, peccasse in uno illo homine: Multo vero minus dixit tunc peccasse cum nondum essent in rerum natura. Hoc enim mihi videtur manifestam contradictionem implicare. Quis enim contradictionem implicari non videat, si quis dicat, prius esse accidens quam subjectum, prius homines fuisse peccatores quam homines, mortuos quam viventes, imo prius peccasse quam fuisse?
